global.headline: IRAN — TRUMP DECLARES CEASEFIRE "OVER" AFTER FRESH HORMUZ ATTACKS; US STRIKES KHARG ISLAND, OIL SURGES
summary: President Trump declared on July 8 that the interim ceasefire agreement with Iran is "over," warning that US retaliation would "get much worse" if Iranian forces keep targeting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. "Every time they hit us, we hit them 20," he said. The declaration followed the July 7 tanker attacks and came hours before CENTCOM confirmed a fresh round of "additional strikes" intended to "further degrade [Iran's] ability to threaten freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz." Iranian state media reported explosions on Kharg Island — which handles roughly 90% of Iran's crude oil exports — as well as at Bandar Abbas, Sirik and Qeshm Island.

Trump said the US would "probably" strike again and floated the possibility of taking Kharg Island outright and reimposing a full blockade on Iranian oil, on top of the Treasury's July 7 revocation of Iran's oil-export waiver (wind-down deadline July 17). Nearly three weeks after the June 17 MOU was signed, the ceasefire it established is now the most damaged it has been since signing.

Oil markets reacted sharply: Brent crude jumped 5.2% to settle at $78.02 a barrel and WTI rose 4.4% to $73.52 — both well above the "near four-month lows" levels reported as recently as July 7, though still short of a full war-premium spike. The International Maritime Organization's chief said nearly 6,000 seafarers remain stranded in the Persian Gulf, and a broader plan to evacuate roughly 11,000 sailors from the region remains paused after a Singapore-flagged container ship was attacked near Oman in late June. Iran is reported to have mined large stretches of Hormuz and, per US officials, may lack the capability to locate or clear all the mines itself.

The escalation unfolded against the backdrop of Khamenei's state funeral: a July 8 procession in Najaf drew an estimated 2.3 million mourners (Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces) before continuing to Karbala, ahead of burial at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad. New Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei did not attend the Iraq processions and, per reporting, was advised against travelling to Mashhad over fears he could be targeted by Israel — his prolonged public absence, tied to leg and facial injuries sustained on the war's first day, remains the central unresolved signal of who is actually directing Iran's response. Foreign ministers from Pakistan and Qatar, Egypt's intelligence chief, Turkey's Erdogan and Saudi officials are reported to be working around the clock to keep the MOU from collapsing outright.
global.geopolitical: Trump calling the ceasefire "over" — rather than formally terminating it — reads to analysts as itself a negotiating tactic, but the practical effect is the same: roughly three weeks into a 60-day MOU, the US is now conducting the most extensive strikes since the funeral period began, and Iran's IRGC is acting with a degree of unilateral latitude that a still-absent Mojtaba Khamenei shows no sign of reining in. The timing lands squarely beside NATO's Ankara declaration, which explicitly calls on Iran to respect freedom of navigation in Hormuz — turning boilerplate alliance language into an immediate live issue. Whether the frantic Pakistani-Qatari-Egyptian-Turkish-Saudi mediation can re-contain this before the funeral period ends and Trump's own rhetoric escalates further is now the central open question.
global.socioeconomic: A 5%+ single-day oil move is the sharpest reaction of this crisis to date, though it remains below true war-premium levels — markets are still pricing containment over collapse, for now. For Singapore, exposure keeps compounding on exposure: STB's already-downgraded S$31–32.5B 2026 tourism forecast, the record Q3 electricity tariff (34.78 cents/kWh with GST, driven by conflict-era gas costs), and now a further-delayed Hormuz reopening (ADNOC had pencilled in "not before 2027") all assumed a durable de-escalation this attack directly undercuts. The stranding of a Singapore-flagged vessel in the evacuation-paused zone in late June underscores that the exposure is not merely macroeconomic.

global.headline: NATO ANKARA DECLARATION ADOPTED, TRUMP OFFERS UKRAINE A PATRIOT-MISSILE PRODUCTION LICENCE — AS RUSSIA HITS KYIV AGAIN
summary: NATO leaders formally endorsed the Ankara summit declaration on July 8, reaffirming Article 5 as "ironclad" and committing to €70B (~SGD 107B) in military assistance to Ukraine for 2026, with allies affirming "at least equivalent" levels for 2027. In a bilateral meeting on the summit sidelines, Trump told Zelenskyy the US will grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture Patriot air-defence interceptors domestically: "We're going to give a license to you to make Patriots. That's pretty cool, right? ... I said, 'Make them yourself.'" Trump acknowledged Lockheed Martin and RTX (formerly Raytheon), which hold the underlying technology, have not yet been informed, and it remains unclear whether production would actually happen inside Ukraine or elsewhere.

Hours after the declaration and the Trump-Zelenskyy meeting, Russia struck Kyiv for a second straight day, killing four people across Ukraine in strikes before dawn and at midday. Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 169 long-range drones and seven missiles, including five ballistic missiles; air defences intercepted or jammed 139 drones, but all five ballistic missiles and 20 drones struck 15 locations. Russia's defence ministry said it hit a plant manufacturing components for Flamingo cruise missiles and a facility assembling mid- and long-range drones.
global.geopolitical: The gap between the summit stage and the battlefield could not have been starker: allies adopted a declaration built around sustaining Ukraine through 2027 within hours of Russian missiles landing on the capital where that declaration's beneficiary lives. The Patriot production licence is a genuine shift toward Ukrainian self-sufficiency in air defence, but with the manufacturers not yet briefed and the manufacturing location undecided, it is a political signal well ahead of an operational plan — its real test comes in how fast (or slowly) it converts into actual interceptors.
global.socioeconomic: The €70B pledge, the Patriot licence, and the forum's separate defence-industrial deals (five Northrop Grumman high-altitude uncrewed aircraft, a five-year $40B counter-drone commitment) all continue channelling European and allied capital into defence production capacity. For Singapore the read-through is structural rather than direct: the RSAF's F-35 programme and its dependence on the same US-European defence-industrial base being renegotiated in Ankara sit downstream of exactly this kind of production-capacity shift.

global.headline: IOC PROVISIONALLY LIFTS RUSSIA'S OLYMPIC SUSPENSION, OPENING PATH BACK FROM LA 2028
summary: The International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its decade-long suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee, opening a pathway for Russian athletes to return as full participants from the 2028 Los Angeles Games onward. The IOC said Russia had addressed the legal basis of the ban — the Russian Olympic Committee formally distanced itself from sports federations in four Ukrainian territories Russia illegally annexed in 2022. Russia's flag and anthem remain banned from international competition "until the appropriate time," and individual sport federations retain discretion over whether to lift their own restrictions, meaning Russian athletes could return to some sports well before others.

Ukraine's foreign ministry called the decision a "troubling signal for the entire international community" and urged federations to keep their own bans in place while Russia's "unprovoked war" continues.
global.geopolitical: Lifting the ban this week — as NATO reaffirms €70B in annual military aid to Ukraine and Russian strikes kill civilians in Kyiv — puts the IOC's institutional logic (procedural compliance by the Russian Olympic Committee) directly at odds with the wartime posture of the alliance funding Ukraine's defence. Devolving the final call to individual federations avoids a single flashpoint but guarantees a drawn-out, sport-by-sport diplomatic fight over the next two years.
global.socioeconomic: Limited direct economic bearing for Singapore; the main consequences are in Olympic broadcast rights, sponsorship, and qualification-pathway logistics for the LA 2028 cycle, which national Olympic committees — including Singapore's — will now need to factor into qualifying-event planning.

global.headline: LE PEN CLEARS PATH TO 2027 PRESIDENTIAL RUN DESPITE EMBEZZLEMENT CONVICTION, ELECTRONIC-MONITOR SENTENCE
summary: France's appeals court reduced Marine Le Pen's original five-year ban on holding office (handed down in March 2025) to 45 months, with two-thirds suspended, over her National Rally party's embezzlement of SGD 4.1M (€2.8M) in European Parliament funds meant for parliamentary assistants over more than 11 years. Le Pen has already served 15 months of the original ban, clearing the practical obstacle to running in 2027. The court separately ordered her to wear an electronic monitor. Le Pen confirmed on July 7 she will contest the 2027 presidency — her fourth run — while also appealing the ruling to France's Court of Cassation, saying the appeal suspends the monitoring order: "I will therefore campaign without an electronic bracelet."
Opponents criticised the decision as the courts effectively clearing a convicted politician to campaign for the presidency.
global.geopolitical: This resolves the single biggest legal uncertainty hanging over the far right's 2027 strategy: Le Pen can now campaign essentially unencumbered while her final appeal plays out, reinforcing National Rally's multi-year normalisation push heading into the campaign.
global.socioeconomic: Direct economic impact is minimal for now, but a serious Le Pen candidacy revives the political-risk premium markets attach to French sovereign debt and EU fiscal-rule compliance whenever her prospects are seen as improving — a dynamic to watch build over the next 18 months.

singapore.headline: TEMASEK REVIEW 2026: NET PORTFOLIO VALUE HITS RECORD S$518B, UP S$49B ON THE YEAR
summary: Temasek's 2026 Annual Review reported net portfolio value of S$518B as at 31 March 2026, up S$49B from the prior year and roughly double its value a decade ago. One-year total shareholder return was 10.5% in SGD terms (14.8% in USD), while 10-year and 20-year TSR held at 7.1% and 6.8% respectively. Temasek invested S$51B and divested S$31B over the financial year, for net investment of S$20B. Since April 1, 2026 the organisation has operated under a restructured model — Temasek Singapore, Temasek Global Investments and Temasek Partnership Solutions — and separately reported S$49B in "sustainable living" investments, up S$3B from 2025.
AI-related exposure currently stands at about 6% of portfolio value, which Temasek said it aims to raise to as much as 15% by 2031.
singapore.geopolitical: As one of Singapore's two sovereign wealth vehicles, Temasek's portfolio composition functions as a proxy for how the state reads global risk: the new three-way split by entity, and the explicit multi-year AI weighting target, signal a deliberate long-horizon positioning within the US-China technology competition rather than a reactive one.
singapore.socioeconomic: A record portfolio print lands the same week as a record COE premium, a softening HDB resale market and Iran-driven cost pressures reported elsewhere in this briefing — underscoring that Temasek's returns and the domestic cost-of-living picture are running on largely separate tracks. The stated AI allocation ramp is the more locally relevant signal: it points toward sustained state capital flowing into AI infrastructure and related sectors through 2031.

singapore.headline: COE PREMIUMS HIT RECORD HIGHS ACROSS CATEGORIES: CAT A $129,000, CAT C $95,000
summary: LTA's July 8 Certificate of Entitlement bidding exercise closed with premiums up across every category. Category A (cars up to 1,600cc/97kW) settled at a record S$129,000, surpassing the previous high of S$128,105 set in October 2025. Category C (goods vehicles and buses) hit a fresh record of S$95,000, above June's S$94,000. Category D (motorcycles) rose to S$10,201, still below its November 2022 peak of S$13,189. The next bidding round opens July 20, with results due July 22.
singapore.geopolitical: Domestic policy matter with no material external dimension this cycle.
singapore.socioeconomic: The record Cat A premium lands the same week as the PARF rebate cut (down 45 percentage points, effective July 1) tightening the economics of upgrading or scrapping a vehicle, and adds to a cost-of-living picture already strained by record Q3 electricity tariffs and 6.0% YoY transport inflation as of April. It gives MAS one more data point to weigh ahead of its July policy meeting on whether a further tightening move is warranted.

singapore.headline: MAN TO BE CHARGED OVER FAKE BOMB THREATS AGAINST HTX, PARLIAMENT HOUSE
summary: Police arrested a 40-year-old man on July 7 over two hoax bomb threats: an online form submission to the Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX) at One-North on July 3, and an anonymous e-mail to the Prime Minister's Office on July 7 claiming a bomb had been placed at Parliament House. Checks at both premises found nothing of security concern. Electronic devices believed used to send the threats were seized. He is set to be charged on July 9 with communicating false information of a harmful thing, an offence carrying up to seven years' jail, a fine of up to S$50,000, or both.
singapore.geopolitical: A domestic law-enforcement matter with no external dimension, though it lands amid a period of elevated global tension that tends to sharpen scrutiny of threats against key government installations.
singapore.socioeconomic: Limited direct economic impact; the case will function as an early test of how firmly the false-information statute is applied against hoax threats to government sites.

singapore.headline: WORKERS' PARTY CEC: FADLI FAWZI, ANDRE LOW CO-OPTED; FAISAL MANAP REAPPOINTED VICE-CHAIR
summary: Following its first meeting on July 7, the Workers' Party confirmed its Central Executive Committee line-up for the new term: Aljunied GRC MP Fadli Fawzi and NCMP Andre Low were co-opted onto the CEC, and Faisal Manap was re-appointed Vice-Chair. Fadli Fawzi retains his post as Deputy Organising Secretary, while Aljunied GRC's Kenneth Tiong takes over as Treasurer from Sengkang GRC's He Ting Ru. Harpreet Singh was the sole new face elected directly to the CEC; party leader Pritam Singh's re-election as Secretary-General was affirmed as the correct outcome.
singapore.geopolitical: Internal party matter with no external bearing.
singapore.socioeconomic: No direct economic impact; the reshuffle is a political signal about the WP's succession bench and organisational continuity heading into the next electoral cycle, rather than a market- or policy-relevant event.

word.definition: The formal or effective cancellation, repeal, or annulment of a law, right, or agreement — often abruptly or unilaterally, without the due process by which it was created.
word.etymology: From Latin abrogatio, from abrogare — ab- ("away, off") + rogare ("to ask, to propose a law"); rogare was the term for formally proposing legislation to the Roman popular assembly, so abrogare meant literally to "un-propose" a law, repealing it by the same process that made it. Entered English legal usage in the 16th century.
word.example: Trump never filed any formal notice ending the June 17 MOU — he simply told reporters the ceasefire was "over" — but three weeks in, with US jets over Kharg Island and Iran's oil waiver revoked, the practical abrogation of the agreement looks complete regardless of the paperwork.
